ring.title: A ring laser feels the ground turn
ring.mini: Two laser beams run around a ring in opposite directions. When the ring turns with the ground, one has further to go: the beams beat at 348.6 Hz at Wettzell, exactly the globe's Ω sin φ. A plane at rest gives 0 Hz.
ring.text: Two light pulses leave the detector together and run around a ring in opposite directions. The ring turns with the ground, so the pulse running with the turn arrives late and the other early. In a ring laser the beams run continuously and the delay shows as interference fringes drifting past the detector at a beat frequency proportional to the rotation about the ring's axis, the local vertical: on a globe, Ω sin φ. Four rings have been measured [1]. Wettzell's 4 m ring G, at 49.1° N, beats at 348.6 Hz; the globe, turning once a sidereal day, predicts 348.6 Hz. The three rings at Christchurch, 43.6° S, from 1 m to 21 × 40 m, beat at 79.4, 1,513 and 2,177 Hz, each within 0.3 % of the globe. A disc turning about its pole would give 32 to 45 % more, a plane at rest none. The ratio of Wettzell to Christchurch, per unit of scale factor, needs no value of Ω: 1.0977 measured, 1.0972 for the ratio of the sines of the two latitudes, 1 for a disc. In the animation the ring's turn during one lap of light is enlarged by about 10¹¹ and the fringes are slowed 200 times.
ring.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a large ring laser whose fringes stand still, or one beating at the same rotation at every latitude.
fall.title: A dropped ball lands east of the plumb line
fall.mini: The top of a deep shaft is further from the Earth's axis than its bottom, so it moves east a few millimetres per second faster. A ball let go at the top keeps that speed: Reich, 1831, measured 28.4 mm east over 158.5 m.
fall.text: Ferdinand Reich dropped balls 106 times down a 158.5 m mine shaft at Freiberg in 1831 [2]. The top of the shaft is further from the Earth's axis than the bottom and is carried east 7.3 mm/s faster; a ball released there keeps that extra speed through its 5.7 s fall and lands east of the plumb line: Reich measured 28.4 ± 0.4 mm, the globe predicts 27.6 mm. Four other series, from Bologna in 1791 to a drop tower in Bremen in 2005, measured the same eastward offset from other heights [1]. Turned around, each gives the rotation rate: the four that agree within three standard deviations give a median of 7.55 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s, against 7.29 × 10⁻⁵ from the stars. On a plane at rest, or a disc turning about a vertical axis, nothing is carried faster at the top and the ball lands on the plumb point. In the animation the fall runs in real time and the eastward offset is enlarged 1,000 times.
fall.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: careful drops from deep shafts landing on the plumb point, with no eastward offset beyond their error.
sid.title: The stars come round four minutes early every day
sid.mini: A star hides behind the same chimney 3 min 56 s earlier every night. The Earth turns once against the stars in 23 h 56 min 4 s, and 366.24 times a year: one turn more than the days, because it also goes around the Sun.
sid.text: Seen from above, the Earth turns and moves along its orbit. Its meridian faces a distant star again after 23 h 56 min 4 s, but faces the Sun again only about four minutes later, because by then the Earth has moved on along its orbit. A camera, a fixed edge such as a chimney and a clock measure it: the same star hides behind the edge 3 min 56 s earlier each night, which adds up to one extra turn in a year, 366.24 turns against the stars for 365.24 days. In the drawing the Earth's daily step along its orbit is enlarged six times so that the gap shows; the times are the true ones.
sid.verdict: Would favour neither model: the sidereal day only fixes the rate at which the sky turns, which a turning dome could copy. It is here as a measurement anyone can make.
